narrative: The model estimated your probability of leaving at 49.0%. That is a borderline estimate—roughly a coin flip—but in this promotion process it was treated as enough retention risk to deny the promotion. The strongest factor in the model’s reasoning was the number of training programs you attended in the last three years. You attended 7 or more, which is more than typical among employees predicted to stay (19.4% in that group), and this factor pushed the prediction toward staying. The second most important factor was that you reported having other job opportunities while in this role. Only 23.3% of employees predicted to stay had outside opportunities, so this pushed the prediction toward leaving. The third factor was your tenure with your current organization: 6–10 years, which is common among employees predicted to stay (34.9% in that group), and it pushed toward staying. Overall, the model saw retention signals in your training history and tenure, but the outside-opportunity signal made your leave risk borderline. Next, you and your organization should discuss your career path and promotion criteria openly, clarify whether the training you received was useful, and address whether outside opportunities reflect unmet growth or satisfaction needs. Because the estimate is close to even, a retention conversation and clearer development plan are more appropriate than treating departure as certain.
